    Industry News: What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov.
    • The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads.
    • However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images).

    The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

    However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

    The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

    Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

    It has been revealed that “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom remarked. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”.

    In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

    Recent findings suggest that black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They revealed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

    When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

    Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

    According to recent reports, keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

    In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

    Industry observers note that I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

    According to recent reports, the number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

    But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

    "I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

    Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

    What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

    Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson proposal?

    Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

    That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

    Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she noted.

    Sources indicate that colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”.

    Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

    I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

    United Airlines' Rare Arctic Flights Only 46% Full: Here's Why

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that united Airlines' ambitious expansion into Greenland has yet to deliver strong passenger numbers.
    • It has been revealed that the opening of Nuuk's latest international airport in November 2024 was intended to transform Greenland's accessibility and stimulate tourism growth.
    • It has been revealed that according to the US Department of Transportation's T-100 data, United transported 3,709 passengers across 48 flights between Newark and Nuuk from June through August.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that united Airlines' ambitious expansion into Greenland has yet to deliver strong passenger numbers. The carrier launched nonstop flights between Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) and Nuuk International Airport (GOH) in June of last year, establishing a unique link between the United States and Greenland. However, in its second summer of operations, load factors deteriorated further, with more than half of its available seats going empty.

    It has been revealed that the opening of Nuuk's latest international airport in November 2024 was intended to transform Greenland's accessibility and stimulate tourism growth. However, inadequate tourism infrastructure, high vacation costs, and a relatively small underlying travel market are among the factors that appear to be limiting demand for United's flights.

    It has been revealed that according to the US Department of Transportation's T-100 data, United transported 3,709 passengers across 48 flights between Newark and Nuuk from June through August. Passenger numbers declined by 5.2% year-over-year despite an 11.6% capacity increase. Consequently, its 166-seat Boeing 737 MAX 8s averaged just 77 passengers per flight, achieving a load factor of 46.5%.

    The figures are particularly concerning when compared with United's broader transatlantic network. Nuuk recorded the lowest load factor by a considerable margin, trailing the service from Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) to Reykjavík's Keflavik International Airport (KEF) by more than 20 percentage points. Even United's other newly introduced European destinations, including Glasgow and Santiago de Compostela, performed substantially better during their first summer.

    Newark – Santiago de Compostela.

    United commenced its second season a week earlier, increasing June capacity by 50% despite passenger numbers declining by 6.1%. This resulted in a particularly poor 32.8% load factor across the month. However, the challenges extend beyond United's scheduling decisions, with Greenland Airports recently acknowledging that insufficient accommodation is constraining aviation growth.

    “Revenue from air traffic is expected to be lower than originally projected, partly because hotel capacity in both Nuuk and Ilulissat continues to be a limiting factor.”.

    It has been revealed that while Greenland has invested heavily in its aviation infrastructure with its newly introduced $300 million airport, its hospitality industry has struggled to keep pace. A 2024 capacity analysis commissioned by Visit Greenland identified just 1,039 available beds across hotels, apartments, and hostels in and around Nuuk. National carrier Air Greenland has also identified accommodation shortages as a significant constraint on further passenger growth.

    It has been revealed that affordability represents another major obstacle. Visit Greenland's 2023 study of Greenland's prospective tourism markets found that 35% of potential North American visitors considered Greenland too expensive. Unlike neighboring Iceland, Greenland has no intercity road network, leaving tourists dependent on relatively expensive domestic flights and boat journeys to explore the country.

    Greenland's small population also means that United cannot rely on the ongoing business and visiting-friends-and-relatives traffic that supports many of its European services. Furthermore, Greenland has an established cruise tourism industry, meaning that growing visitor numbers do not automatically translate into additional demand for scheduled international flights.

    Industry observers note that united's twice-weekly schedule also limits itinerary flexibility, particularly given Greenland's susceptibility to weather-related flight disruptions. Despite requiring a connection, Icelandair's Greenland network offers more frequent service and access to four destinations, potentially providing a more attractive alternative for travelers who want to explore beyond Nuuk or combine Greenland and Iceland in a single vacation.

    Geopolitical uncertainty may also have contributed to weaker demand in 2026. President Donald Trump's ambitions to acquire Greenland generated considerable international attention during the important early-year booking period. However, while some tour operators reported declining bookings, others experienced increased interest, making it difficult to establish whether the political situation adversely affected United's flights.

    Bookings down 20%, but a subsequent increase in inquiries.

    Increased interest from US, UK and German travelers.

    The recent openings of international airports at Qaqortoq and Ilulissat should support Greenland's longer-term tourism ambitions. However, from January 1, 2027, Greenland Airports is more than doubling its summer international passenger fee to DKK 1,182 ($171), further challenging affordability. Ironically, the justification for the increase is that revenue has come in lower than projected, “partly because hotel capacity in both Nuuk and Ilulissat continues to be a limiting factor.”.

    In a recent development, the reality is that United has solved the challenge of getting Americans to Greenland, but Greenland has not yet solved the challenges of accommodating them, transporting them around the island, and making their vacations affordable. So while United's Greenland services remain scheduled for 2027, achieving sustainable performance will require considerable effort to stimulate stronger demand or adjustments to fare structures and capacity.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that in May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed, so that it could undergo a renovation.
    • The hotel is expected to reopen in the spring of 2027, and the first pictures of the latest room product have just been revealed, as flagged by rota.
    • Dubai is a city that has endless hotels at all price points.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that in May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed, so that it could undergo a renovation. That was probably good timing, given the massively decreased demand we’ve seen for travel to the United Arab Emirates this year.

    The hotel is expected to reopen in the spring of 2027, and the first pictures of the latest room product have just been revealed, as flagged by rota. Let’s take a look at those details, but first, I’d like to briefly talk about why I have a soft spot for this property.

    Dubai is a city that has endless hotels at all price points. I don’t have a single favorite hotel in the city, as it really depends on so many factors, from what you’re willing to pay, to the area you want to be in, to how major you want the property to be, to what you value most.

    After all, the concept of hotels in Dubai is a bit different than in other cities, given that alcohol is primarily only served at restaurants in hotels. As a result, hotels are very much the social scenes, both for guests and non-guests.

    It has been revealed that anyway, the 223-key Park Hyatt Dubai opened all the way back in 2005, and I can’t count how many times I’ve stayed there over the years, going back to just shortly after it initially opened. There’s a lot to like about the resort:.

    To me, it very much fits into the category of being an urban resort, in terms of being a destination, while having ideal proximity to things.

    Recent findings suggest that there are just some hotels where you have such fond memories for a variety of reasons, and for me, the Park Hyatt Dubai is definitely among them. In part, maybe it can’t help but remind me of the “good old days” of redeeming Alaska Mileage Proposal miles for Emirates first class.

    Remember being able to redeem 100,000 Alaska miles for Emirates first class from the US to basically anywhere in the world via Dubai, with a free stopover there, and no carrier imposed surcharges? And that claims nothing of being able to fly from the US to London with a stopover in Mauritius, and layovers in Dubai twice on a one-way (IYKYK). 😉.

    In May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed for the main portion of its renovation. If you go to the hotel’s website, you’ll see the following restrictions:.

    Park Hyatt Dubai is currently closed as it embarks on a defining transformation – a moment of careful, considered renewal in pursuit of an experience that is more refined, more exceptional, and more authentically itself than ever before.

    Behind the scenes, every space and every detail is being thoughtfully elevated – honouring the quality and commitment to luxury hospitality that have made this sanctuary on Dubai Creek so singular, while reimagining the perfect stay.

    With an anticipated reopening date of Q1 2027, we look forward to sharing more updates as that moment approaches, and to welcoming you back to a truly reawakened Park Hyatt Dubai. Because true elegance never stands still. It evolves – and in evolving, it is perfected.

    As it currently stands, the hotel is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. Now, the hotel is accepting villa reservations as of January 1, 2027, but that’s separate from the main part of the hotel. We’ve known that everything about the hotel would change, but not many renderings had been shared up until now.

    One thing is for sure — there’s no denying that the rooms were in desperate need of a renovation, given that they hadn’t undergone any meaningful updates since the hotel first opened.

    The hotel has now updated its website to show pictures of the new room product, and you can find those renderings below. I’m conflicted here. On the one hand, this looks much more luxurious than the old setup. On the other hand, the design just looks incredibly generic, and like it could be anywhere. I wish we’d see a little more sense of place.

    On the plus side, the hotel’s grounds and general bones otherwise have a decent sense of place, so I hope that’s at least maintained with the updates.

    Sources indicate that leadership at the Park Hyatt Dubai had been vocal about how they hope to charge much higher rates after the renovation. I think it’s safe to say that’s all up in the air, based on how the situation in the Middle East evolves. As things right now stand, I see entry level rates in April that are $600+, while I see the lowest rates in summer at $350+.

    I feel like that pricing is very much on the optimistic side, but again, there are lots of moving parts with the Middle East hotel situation.

    The Park Hyatt Dubai closed in May 2026, and is currently undergoing a full renovation. In recent years we’ve seen a new beach club and new dining outlets added, but this should be by far the most meaningful update since the hotel opened over two decades ago.

    The hotel is expected to fully reopen in April 2027, and the fresh rooms look like a huge improvement in terms of how luxurious they are. However, there’s definitely a sense of place missing, so I’m curious how the overall design evolves.

    What do you make of the changes coming to the Park Hyatt Dubai?

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

    I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly announced at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero. However, the airline has now released a video on social media with additional details, so I’d like to publish an update to reflect that.

    To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet presently consists of 25 planes, including:.

    Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was revealed by the company’s CEO at last week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

    Sources indicate that the proposal is for the 787-9s to get all-new cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

    Recent findings suggest that the 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the cabins will be updated between 2029 and 2031, so that’s between three and five years from now (and that assumes no additional delays).

    We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

    The plane will also have 69% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the fresh premium economy cabin.

    It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

    Aeromexico’s fresh premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

    Aeromexico has published the below video about its all-newly introduced cabins, which gives you a sense of what we can expect.

    A post shared by Aeroméxico (@aeromexico).

    For those who don’t want to watch the video, below are some screen grabs.

    Side note — is this new, or has Aeromexico been doing a cute tequila service for a long time?!? If I knew Aeromexico was serving shots, I would’ve prioritized the airline much higher on my list of products to review. 😉.

    According to recent reports, while details are otherwise limited, we know that Aeromexico’s latest Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new seat. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

    I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

    It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the latest Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

    It has been revealed that aeromexico is planning some significant upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-latest cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

    As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these upcoming cabins to roll out between 2029 and 2031, so unfortunately patience will be required.

    • A judge remarked he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep.
    • Industry observers note that judge James Boasberg for the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    A judge remarked he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

    Industry observers note that judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

    “This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

    The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

    In a recent development, boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he mentioned next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

    Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”.

    The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

    “You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

    Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

    Separately, Boasberg remarked he may glitch rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

    The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

    For years Trump has stated he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

    Why Southwest Airlines Likely Won't Fly The Boeing 737 MAX 8-200 Like Allegiant Air & Ryanair

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that southwest Airlines has not publicly issued a formal explanation for why it does not operate the 737 MAX 8-200, but its commercial direction in 2026 points straight toward the underlying reason.
    • Contrasting Southwest against ultra-low-cost operators such as Ryanair and Allegiant Air indicates how the same Boeing 737 MAX family can serve massively different commercial models.
    • The 737 MAX 8-200 is a high-density derivative of the standard 737 MAX 8 created to help ultra-low-cost operators push seat counts on single-aisle routes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that southwest Airlines has not publicly issued a formal explanation for why it does not operate the 737 MAX 8-200, but its commercial direction in 2026 points straight toward the underlying reason. The 8-200 is engineered to pack maximum seating density into a single-aisle cabin, whereas Southwest has spent 2026 reshaping its cabin experience around assigned seating, extra-legroom rows, new fare tiers, and upcoming Icon lounges. If an airline moves away from open-seating boarding toward structured comfort and paid upgrades, squeezing 15 to 20 extra seats onto every aircraft works directly against that strategy.

    Contrasting Southwest against ultra-low-cost operators such as Ryanair and Allegiant Air indicates how the same Boeing 737 MAX family can serve massively different commercial models. Ryanair configures its 8-200 jets for maximum seat count, Allegiant pairs high-capacity seating with extra-legroom rows, and Southwest keeps 175 seats across its standard 737 MAX 8 and 737-800 aircraft. The way in which the 8-200 is designed, how carriers like Ryanair and Allegiant use it, and how Southwest's 2026 product shift unfolds explains why the Dallas-based carrier is unlikely to chase maximum-density narrowbody layouts.

    The 737 MAX 8-200 is a high-density derivative of the standard 737 MAX 8 created to help ultra-low-cost operators push seat counts on single-aisle routes. As One Mile At A Time notes, the variant keeps the same fuselage length, overall airframe dimensions, engines, maximum takeoff weight, and range capability as a baseline 737 MAX 8. Contrary to a standard stretching of the airframe or altering core flight performance, Boeing focused on regulatory evacuation thresholds and interior floor-space efficiency so airlines could carry more passengers per flight.

    Industry observers note that for the allowance of higher passenger loads while meeting evacuation rules, Boeing added an extra pair of emergency exit doors behind the wing on the 737 MAX 8-200. Reporting from Aviation Week explains that this mid-cabin exit modification raised the design capacity from the standard 737 MAX 8 ceiling up to 200 seats initially, with later configurations reaching up to 210 seats. Across Europe, aviation rules cap the 737 MAX 8-200 at 202 passengers, forming a strict ceiling even in high-demand short-haul markets.

    Achieving those higher seat totals comes from the design of the high-density 8-200 configuration rather than any single airline's livery or onboard branding. As highlighted in Simple Flying analysis, packing additional rows into a single-aisle cabin of roughly 11 feet 7 inches (approximately 3.53 meters) in width means using slimline seats, tighter seat pitch, compact lavatories, and reduced galley space. Those hardware and floorplan choices lower cost per seat on paper, but they leave far less room for cabin comfort or generous legroom.

    Ryanair is the clearest real-world example of the 737 MAX 8-200 deployed strictly as a high-density, low-fare machine across busy short-haul European routes. As shown in trip reports from WillAviation, Ryanair fits 197 slimline seats spaced at 28 inches (approximately 71.1 centimeters) of pitch, the distance from one seat back to the next, compared with 189 seats on its older 737-800 aircraft. Adding eight extra seats per jet spreads fixed operating costs across more fare-paying flyers on high-frequency point-to-point sectors.

    Industry observers note that squeezing 197 seats into that single-aisle cabin, Ryanair leans on interior space compromises tailored to ultra-low-cost operations. The layout relies on three small lavatories and removes some galley space, trading onboard amenity space and restroom capacity for lower cost per seat, as noted by Simple Flying. On short European flights built around rock-bottom base fares and rapid turnarounds, maximizing seat count per departure takes clear priority over extra cabin room.

    As the 737 MAX 8-200's main operator by a wide margin, Ryanair demonstrates how directly the variant supports an ultra-low-cost business model. Packing 197 seats into the airframe helps lower per-seat costs across high-frequency schedules, so that Ryanair does not have to step up to a larger aircraft type and change its single-type business model.

    According to recent reports, allegiant Air takes a slightly more segmented approach to the 737 MAX 8-200, combining high overall passenger capacity with a dedicated block of extra-legroom seats aimed at leisure travelers. As One Mile At A Time reports, Allegiant configures its 737 MAX 8-200 aircraft with 190 seats, including 21 extra-legroom Allegiant Extra seats. That cabin arrangement allows flyers who want extra space to pay a little extra for it but keep the total seat count substantially higher than a standard narrowbody layout.

    Sources indicate that for a leisure-focused airline whose routes center on vacation and seasonal demand, having high-capacity rows and paid legroom upgrades has a clear commercial role. Reporting from One Mile At A Time notes that Allegiant Extra seating provides at least six inches (approximately 15.2 centimeters) of extra pitch over standard rows, paired with power ports and larger overhead bins. Even with those extra-legroom seats built into the cabin, the 190-seat total remains a high-density narrowbody setup.

    Sources indicate that comparing Allegiant's 190-seat layout against Ryanair's 197-seat configuration shows how airlines adapt the same 737 MAX 8-200 airframe to different revenue strategies. Both carriers take advantage of the 8-200's high-density capability to boost passenger volume per flight, but Allegiant sets aside 21 seats for extra-legroom upsells, not chasing the highest possible seat count across every row. Even with that nuance, Allegiant's leisure-driven density sits well apart from Southwest's evolving cabin model.

    It has been revealed that southwest Airlines moves in the opposite direction from maximum-density narrowbody layouts, offering 175 seats on its standard 737 MAX 8 and 737-800 aircraft. As reported by Travel Weekly, Southwest has reconfigured jets to sell extra-legroom seats with 34 to 36 inches (approximately 86.4 to 91.4 centimeters) of pitch up front, while keeping standard seats at 31 inches (approximately 78.7 centimeters). That standard seat pitch already gives flyers roughly one inch (approximately 2.5 centimeters) more legroom than many flights on American, Delta, and United.

    Recent findings suggest that squeezing 15 to 20 additional seats onto a Southwest 737, the jump from 175 seats into the 190-to-197-seat range seen on high-density layouts, would clash directly with that seating structure. Tighter row spacing or trimmed cabin spaces would take away the comfort edge Southwest is building across its extra-legroom rows and standard seats throughout the main cabin. Adding extra seats simply to chase peak density would undermine the legroom differentiation meant to win over higher-yielding domestic travelers.

    Those cabin geometry trade-offs carry real weight for an airline that spent decades operating uniform single-class cabins with fast turns. Integrating 34-to-36-inch (approximately 86.4-to-91.4-centimeter) extra-legroom pitch and 31-inch (approximately 78.7-centimeter) standard pitch in a way that does not massively affect overall seat count is what shapes cabin layout, passenger comfort, and fare revenue across every flight. Keeping a 175-seat setup protects the legroom and seat segmentation Southwest now relies on across its fleet.

    Southwest Airlines' recent cabin evolution has stemmed from a repositioning away from its old no-frills open-seating identity toward structured choices and elevated customer touchpoints. Highlighted in Simple Flying coverage, initiatives such as assigned seating, extra legroom rows, upcoming premium fare types, and upcoming Icon lounges signal an airline reshaping how travelers experience the brand across its network. In that context, an ultra-dense narrowbody cabin designed around bare-bones squeezing projects the wrong brand message.

    Recent findings suggest that customer perception and onboard atmosphere matter just as much as seat counts when an airline is actively rebranding its travel experience. Moving from open boarding to assigned seats and tiered fare options changes what flyers expect from the moment they book through boarding and lounge access. A cabin geared toward maximum crowding conflicts with a brand leaning into comfort, structure, and hospitality across every stage of the journey.

    According to recent reports, that brand shift mirrors a wider divide across commercial aviation between ultra-low-cost carriers pushing maximum density and airlines moving toward more space and premium options. Ryanair, Allegiant, VietJet, and Akasa Air have all committed to the 737 MAX 8-200, while airlines such as Southwest and United favor the standard 737 MAX 8 with fewer seats. Together, those opposing camps show why Southwest's brand direction ultimately points away from the 8-200.

    Recent findings suggest that taken together, the 737 MAX 8-200 illustrates how a single airframe family can pull in opposite commercial directions depending on how an airline values seat volume versus cabin space. While the 8-200 gives ultra-low-cost and high-density operators extra exit capacity to push seat counts up to 197 or 190, Southwest Airlines has moved away from maximum squeezing toward assigned seating, extra-legroom rows, newly introduced premium fare tiers, and upcoming Icon lounges. Holding on to 175 seats on its standard 737 MAX 8 and 737-800 aircraft aligns naturally with that space-led shift, whereas packing 15 to 20 extra seats onto each jet would undermine the comfort edge Southwest is building.

    Sources indicate that found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

    Ultimately, Southwest does not need to publicly explain away the 737 MAX 8-200 for its fleet logic to come into sharp focus for travelers and industry watchers across the market. A high-density variant engineered to maximize seat count per departure simply does not match an airline repositioning around extra space, structured seating, and higher-tier customer touchpoints. Unless Southwest reverses course and abandons that 2026 product direction in favor of ultra-low-cost crowding across its single-aisle fleet, the 737 MAX 8-200 is unlikely to find a place in its aircraft lineup.

While this includes all kinds of updates, the two biggest developments are the opening of two new terminals — we’re talking about Terminal 6 and Terminal One (not to be confused with Terminal 1).

    As you’d expect, the opening of both terminals has been delayed, since airport construction rarely runs on time. Per the latest updates, the expectation is that Terminal 6 will open before the end of 2026, while Terminal One will open in the first quarter of 2027.

    Along those lines, it’s looking like we might just be days away from the opening of Terminal 6, so I’d like to cover all the details we know.

    Recent findings suggest that JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open with a phased approach as of December 2026. To cover the very basics:.

    The below video of the terminal should give you a good sense of what to expect in terms of the passenger experience, so I’d recommend checking that out.

    All things considered, this new terminal moving is awesome, given the quality of terminals at JFK otherwise. For those originating or terminating in New York, this should be ideal. For those connecting to or from JetBlue in Terminal 5, this will also make connections much easier. Meanwhile for a limited number of other passengers, this might make connections a bit more complicated, for cases where airlines are moving away from their partners (like Cathay Pacific moving from American’s Terminal 8 to Terminal 6).

    Industry observers note that roughly 17 airlines are expected to eventually operate out of JFK Terminal 6, though that will happen in two phases. Broadly speaking, we’ll see some JetBlue operations move there (since the airline is a core tenant), and on top of that, we’ll largely see airlines move from Terminal 1, Terminal 7, and Terminal 8.

    So the expectation is that the following airlines will eventually operate from JFK Terminal 6:.

    There is still a bit of a mystery as to the order in which airlines will move to JFK Terminal 6. For one, there’s the two phases of the terminal opening, but even within each phase, it won’t fully be overnight.

    In a recent development, we know that All Nippon Airways, Cathay Pacific, Condor, Frontier, Lufthansa Group carriers, and TAP Air Portugal, will move in the first phase. Meanwhile we know that Air India will move in the second phase. But for the remainder of the airlines, there’s a lack of certainty on that front.

    Sources indicate that now, we’ll see if this sticks, and how accurate it is, but current schedule filings suggest that Condor will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 3, while Cathay Pacific will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 15 (thanks to Peter_ for flagging this). So it sounds like we could potentially be just over a week from the first airline moving, which would be awesome!

    In terms of lounges, we have confirmation that Terminal 6 will have outposts from Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, Aer Lingus, and Air India. Hopefully the latest lounges are ready to go as airlines make the move, but I wouldn’t consider that to be a sure thing, given the complexity of airport operations.

    It has been revealed that the Air India lounge definitely won’t open anytime soon, since the airline is only moving in the second phase. Meanwhile the Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, and Aer Lingus lounges, will hopefully open soon(ish). Of course I’m most excited to see what Cathay Pacific has in store, given its amazing lounge quality.

    JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open before the end of 2026, and if current filings are to be believed, the move could happen as soon as early December. It appears that Condor and Cathay Pacific might be among the first airlines to move, so hopefully Cathay Pacific’s new lounge isn’t too far behind. So we’ll mark this as “developing,” but the completion of the first exciting phase of this $19 billion project is imminent.

    “I stated, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

    Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

    “My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he noted.

Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that an American Airlines flight traveling from San Diego International Airport (SAN) to Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) was diverted to Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) overnight following a serious onboard security incident.
    • While initial reports suggested that the passenger attempted to breach the cockpit, according to AIRLIVE, police have yet to confirm which aircraft door was targeted.
    • AA1494 departed San Diego late on Tuesday evening, and according to flight tracking data, the overnight service was operated by an Airbus A321 registered N568UW, according to Planespotters.net.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that an American Airlines flight traveling from San Diego International Airport (SAN) to Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) was diverted to Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) overnight following a serious onboard security incident. According to ABC 15 Arizona, air traffic controllers reported a "Level 3 threat" aboard the aircraft, with cabin crew and passengers restraining a disruptive passenger before the aircraft landed safely.

    While initial reports suggested that the passenger attempted to breach the cockpit, according to AIRLIVE, police have yet to confirm which aircraft door was targeted. Federal regulations impose strict requirements on airlines to safeguard their flight decks, and several passengers who have attempted to gain unauthorized access to cockpits in recent years have subsequently been sentenced to federal prison and substantial fines.

    AA1494 departed San Diego late on Tuesday evening, and according to flight tracking data, the overnight service was operated by an Airbus A321 registered N568UW, according to Planespotters.net. The 13-year-old aircraft originally entered service with US Airways before joining American's fleet after the merger of the two carriers.

    According to recent reports, the Phoenix Police Department said preliminary findings indicated that a male passenger had disregarded repeated instructions from flight attendants and attempted to interfere with an aircraft door. Initially, this was reported as an attempted breach of the cockpit door, but subsequent ATC recordings obtained via X suggest the unruly passenger might have tried to open door R in the forward cabin, triggering an alarm. Authorities have yet to confirm whether it was one or both of these doors.

    Video footage recorded by passengers demonstrated the individual being restrained, while police confirmed that both passengers and crew members were involved in subduing him.

    Industry observers note that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirmed that the aircraft landed safely in Phoenix, where law enforcement officers removed the passenger. It also said that the FBI has been notified of the incident and confirmed that it will investigate. According to Arizona's Family, the individual was taken to the hospital with a minor injury, while no other injuries were reported.

    “We want to thank our team members for their professionalism, as well as our customers for their assistance and understanding,” American said in a statement.

    Industry observers note that the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) classifies onboard security threats into four levels of increasing severity. In February 2026, the International Federation of Air Line Pilots' Associations (IFALPA) and the International Federation of Air Traffic Controllers' Associations (IFATCA) called for wider adoption of the framework to improve coordination between airlines, flight crews, air traffic controllers, and law enforcement agencies.

    Suspicious conduct or verbal threats.

    Physical aggression toward other occupants.

    Conduct that endangers human life.

    Attempted or actual unauthorized cockpit entry.

    Recent findings suggest that notably, an attempted cockpit breach would ordinarily constitute a Level 4 threat, and the fact that ATC reported a Level 3 threat further supports the theory that the unruly passenger was tampering with door R. Either way, it represented an unacceptable risk to the aircraft and its passengers, which fully supports the pilot's decision to divert.

    According to recent reports, according to the FAA, the captain is responsible for the safety of the aircraft, its passengers, and crew. Federal regulations also grant captains considerable emergency authority, including the ability to deviate from standard operating procedures when necessary to safeguard the aircraft. While publicly available regulations do not mandate an automatic diversion for every threat classification, captains will usually divert when continued flight presents an unacceptable safety risk.

    American experienced a similar incident in February 2022, when AA1775 from Los Angeles to Washington, DC, diverted to Kansas City. According to the Associated Press (AP), the passenger attempted to access the cockpit and open an aircraft exit. In July 2024, Juan Rivas was sentenced to 19 months in federal prison and ordered to pay American Airlines $64,434 in restitution.

    $7,500 fine, civil penalties and three years of supervised release.

    Over $73,000 restitution and one year of supervised release.

    One of the most recent convictions involved a Swiss International Air Lines flight that returned to Newark in March 2024 following an attempted cockpit breach and assaults on cabin crew. In June 2026, Belgian passenger Jan Daeninck was sentenced to 10 months in prison. The case also highlights the considerable financial consequences for offenders, with Daeninck ordered to pay more than $73,000 in restitution.

    Recent findings suggest that while the federal prison sentences in these four recent cases ranged from 10 to 19 months, US law allows for considerably harsher punishment. Interference with flight crew members through assault or intimidation carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, with even more severe penalties possible under certain circumstances. Whether the passenger aboard AA1494 faces federal prosecution will depend on the findings of the ongoing investigation.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia. It’s an area where Delta has increasingly fallen behind United in recent years, but Delta now hopes to not only catch up, but even beat United. We’ll see what comes of that, and in particular, find out just how costly that growth is.

    A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed prepares to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan. Executives also confirmed out of which airport the service would operate. There’s now an additional update, as an announcement about the new route is imminent, which almost certainly points to a fall 2027 launch for the service.

    As Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. So, what kind of expansion should we expect?

    Sources indicate that back in August 2026, Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito explicitly confirmed that the airline would return to Singapore. What was perhaps most interesting is that he also indirectly confirmed the hub out of which the service would operate — Esposito ruled out that the service could operate out of Los Angeles, so it’s pretty clear that the airline will operate this service out of Seattle (SEA).

    That’s also what JonNYC reported in the past, and now we can take that a step further — Delta is holding an event in Seattle in early December 2026, and that’s when the airline is expected to announce the service.

    Sources indicate that my guess is that we’re looking at a fall 2027 service start, at best. At 8,070 miles, this will be Delta’s third longest flight, after its routes to South Africa, which are from Atlanta (ATL) to Cape Town (CPT) and Johannesburg (JNB).

    According to recent reports, one certainly wonders if this Singapore route could be operated by Delta’s latest Airbus A350-1000s, which will feature an all-new passenger experience. While the plane has great range and per seat economics, the only thing I’d say is that it’s “a lot of plane” for a new market, in terms of the overall capacity (even with the very premium layout).

    Industry observers note that in both the Seattle and Los Angeles to Singapore market, Singapore Airlines is the only other carrier operating. So competitively there’s not a huge difference in that regard, though Los Angeles is a significantly larger market in terms of demand for Singapore, and for that matter, Singapore Airlines also has more service out of the airport. But perhaps Delta is also looking to beat Alaska to the punch in the Seattle market.

    Industry observers note that it’s fantastic to see Delta looking to grow its presence in Asia. Point-to-point flying to Asia is a market that United has basically had cornered in recent years, and competition is good for consumers.

    It’s amazing to think for how many years Delta basically squandered its Asia advantage. Keep in mind that back in the day, Northwest had a robust Asia network, and after the merger with Delta, we saw that network decreased slowly but steadily, as Delta instead focused on routing everything through Seoul Incheon, and into the Korean Air network. So I’m happy to see a reversal of that strategy.

    Sources indicate that I also have to say that given Delta’s hubris, it’s kind of fun to see the airline having to increasingly play “catch up,” rather than coming in as the dominant carrier. And I think that very much sums up what’s going on in Asia.

    The most basic structural disadvantage that Delta has is that United has a fortress hub in San Francisco (SFO), which is where a large part of its Asia network flies from. That’s fantastic for connectivity, not to mention San Francisco is a very strong market for Asia traffic.

    Delta, meanwhile, is taking a split hub approach, flying out of both Los Angeles and Seattle. Obviously Delta is trying to make the best of its situation, but there’s no denying that this is an uphill battle:.

    In a recent development, it also has to be emphasized that in terms of actually transporting passengers profitably (or at less of a loss), United does a better job at that than Delta, despite its lower overall profitability. Comparing passenger revenue per air seat mile to cost per air seat mile, United is at 16.18 cents vs. 16.46 cents, while Delta is at 17.37 cents vs. 19.31 cents.

    Delta is growing quite a bit in Asia at the moment. The airline has already launched flights to Hong Kong, with flights now on sale to Manila and Tokyo Narita. On top of that, Delta is expected to announce a new Seattle to Singapore route within the next two weeks, with a launch likely planned for the fall of 2027.

    It’s great for passengers to see more competition across the Pacific, as Delta sure is making up for a lack of effort for years. However, the airline will also have quite the disadvantage compared to United for a long time….

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025.
    • Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.
    • The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

    The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

    Zinke’s wife, son, and sister presently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

    In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he remarked when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

    The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke remarked.

    None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

    “While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

    Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

    Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

    “I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

    “Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

    Recent findings suggest that zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

    According to recent reports, it marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

    The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with intends to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

    Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

    Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

    Recent findings suggest that zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

    The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

    Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

    Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

    The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

    According to recent reports, SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

    In a recent development, since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s organization, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

    Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

    Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

    “We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he stated, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

    SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

    Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

    In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

    The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

    Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

    It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

    “If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail stated about SEAL PAC's payments.

    But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

    Airbus A380 Fuel Burn: How 4 Engines Shape The Superjumbo’s Economics

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This October, the Federal Aviation Administration sent a harsh reminder to Airbus A380-800 operators about the cost of four-engine complexity.
    • Emirates refuses to treat the double-decker as an operational liability.
    • Because four-engine aircraft consume almost twice as much fuel per hour as a contemporary twinjet and require twice as many shop visits when external maintenance facilities stop, most airline planners steer clear of these aircraft.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This October, the Federal Aviation Administration sent a harsh reminder to Airbus A380-800 operators about the cost of four-engine complexity. After an uncontained high-pressure turbine seal failure caused an engine shutdown and an aborted takeoff, the FAA directed the Engine Alliance GP7200 turbofans, which power many of the superjumbos, to be recalled from service for overhaul. Replacing each sub-assembly costs up to $528,150 per engine, demonstrating how four large powerplants compound mechanical difficulties and high hourly fuel costs.

    Emirates refuses to treat the double-decker as an operational liability. During its financial year ended in March, the Dubai carrier posted a record $6.2 billion pretax profit and bought out 29 leased A380-800s outright to keep them flying into the 2040s. The airline's leadership openly acknowledged that the superjumbo was the most profitable asset in its whole fleet, wagering billions on multi-class cabin repairs while almost all other international operators scrapped the type.

    Because four-engine aircraft consume almost twice as much fuel per hour as a contemporary twinjet and require twice as many shop visits when external maintenance facilities stop, most airline planners steer clear of these aircraft. Emirates packs high-paying fliers into slot-choked international airports where additional daily flights are not feasible, turning an out-of-production giant into its top earner nonetheless.

    According to recent reports, an Airbus A350-1000 consumes 1,823 gallons (6,900 liters) of jet fuel per hour, whereas four Rolls-Royce Trent 900 or GP7200 turbofans consume about 4,600 gallons (17,413 liters). By cramming up to 600 passengers into slot-rationed hubs like London Heathrow and New York-JFK, Emirates reverses that fuel penalty. At slot-capped airports where Emirates cannot get a second takeoff slot, a single 85%-full A380 carries nearly twice as many high-fare passengers as one 787-9, easily paying for the extra fuel.

    Recent findings suggest that while small subfleets decimated rivals in Europe, Dubai's fleet size made it viable. Clark said in November 2019, according to Airline Ratings:.

    It has been revealed that "The A380 was a misfit for Air France. They never scaled, they only have ten aircraft. Yes, we faced the same teething problems, but we dealt with them because we were scaled enough to deal with it. If you've got a sub fleet of 10 it's a bloody nightmare and the costs go through the roof.".

    Industry observers note that running over a hundred quadjets in-house spreads fixed tooling and spare-engine costs over a large number of daily flying hours. Nonetheless, four engines penalize timetables whenever external repair shops fail. By October, 24 Emirates superjumbos had been parked and seven stored due to engine overhauls, while 84 had flown, exposing an older rift within Dubai's dual-engine sourcing policy that helped doom the assembly line.

    Emirates powered its first 90 Airbus A380-800s with GP7200 engines before stunning manufacturers in April 2015 with a $9.2 billion switch to Rolls-Royce Trent 900 turbofans for its final 50 jets. Fine desert sand around Dubai quickly accelerated fan blade wear, delaying deliveries by months and sparking years of haggling that forced Emirates to slash 39 superjumbo orders in February 2019, leaving Airbus CEO Tom Enders without enough backlog to sustain production.

    Enders shut down the Toulouse assembly line because selling low volumes below production cost made no financial sense, commenting to NPR: "If you have a product that nobody wants anymore, or you can only sell only below production cost, you have to stop it, as painful as it is." Even so, Clark still campaigns for a modernized A380neo, arguing that next-generation engines and composite wings would cut hourly fuel burn from 26,455 pounds (12 metric tons) to 19,842 pounds (9 metric tons).

    Airbus declined until commitments reached about 250 aircraft, despite Clark's insistence that Emirates purchase at least 100 modified superjumbos to enable ultra-long-haul flights from Dubai to Santiago and São Paulo. As MigFlug covered, Clark went on the record, saying: "I'm telling you, we would purchase them if you cross-fertilized A350 or 787 technology into a fresh A380, which would result in a 25% reduction in operating expenses. A minimum (order) of one hundred is required.".

    It has been revealed that four engines used to be an airline's best insurance policy over open water, but modern reliability turned that extra hardware into dead weight. Quadjets lost their ocean monopoly overnight when regulators allowed twinjets, such as the Airbus A350-1000 and Boeing 777-300ER, to fly for six hours on a single engine. On almost all long-haul routes, newer twin-engine widebodies also reduce fuel consumption per seat by 25% to 30%, rendering four-engine aircraft obsolete.

    Industry observers note that maintaining four intricate turbofans increases mechanical wear on additional turbine blades and fuel pumps, resulting in maintenance expenditures for the Airbus A380-800 exceeding $6,000 per hour and overall operating expenses of $30,000 per flight hour or more. The FAA's October directive regarding Engine Alliance GP7200 engines demonstrated the high expense of those additional parts. The agency warned in the Federal Register:.

    "Although the root cause is still under investigation, HPT interstage mid-seal clocking has been identified as a contributing factor for the failure... The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in an engine fire and damage to the airplane.".

    Doubling the engine count also increases a fleet's vulnerability to rare, catastrophic manufacturing flaws. In November 2010, Qantas Flight 32 experienced a massive Rolls-Royce Trent 900 explosion over Indonesia after a fractured pipe wall thinner than 0.02 inches (0.5 mm) shattered a turbine disk and severed 650 wing wires. Seven years later, Air France Flight 66 lost an outboard GP7200 fan hub over Greenland at 37,000 feet (11,278 meters) because microscopic strain cracked the forged titanium.

    In a recent development, due to weight and simple aerodynamics, two large engines outperform four smaller ones. Compared to the Airbus A380-800's four smaller GP7200 or Rolls-Royce Trent 900 pods, modern twinjets like the Airbus A350-1000 and Boeing 777-9 have enormous composite fans beneath each wing that drive massive columns of slower air with far less drag. Additionally, the wing loses thousands of pounds of structural weight and friction when two engine housings and pylons are cut.

    Recent findings suggest that airbus built 25% of the superjumbo from lightweight composites and cutting-edge metals to counteract the weight penalty of four engines. Engineers constructed aviation's first carbon-composite center wing box, saving 3,307 pounds (1.5 metric tons), and topped the fuselage with GLARE aluminum-glass laminates to stop fatigue cracks. Underneath, dropped-hinge wing flaps sealed trailing-edge gaps, so air flowed smoothly across the massive 261.8-foot (79.8-meter) wingspan during high-altitude cruise.

    Engine Alliance GP7200 (A380-861).

    116-inch (2.96-meter) fan; 14,811 pounds (6,718 kg) dry.

    74,735 to 80,290 pounds of thrust (332.4 to 357.1 kN); 8.7:1 bypass; 36.92:1 pressure ratio.

    Pairs nine-stage GE90 core with hollow titanium fan.

    Rolls-Royce Trent 900 (A380-841/-842).

    116-inch (2.95-meter) fan; 13,770 pounds (6,246 kg) dry.

    69,691 to 80,931 pounds of thrust (310 to 360 kN); 8.7:1 bypass; 37 to 39:1 pressure ratio.

    Three-shaft design with contra-rotating spool (+2% efficiency).

    97,000 pounds of thrust (431 kN); 9.6:1 bypass; 50:1 pressure ratio.

    Higher core pressure cuts per-seat fuel burn 25% to 30%.

    134-inch (3.40-meter) composite fan.

    105,000 pounds of thrust (467 kN); 10:1 bypass; 60:1 pressure ratio.

    Massive twin fan diameters replace two extra engine pods.

    Blending stiff carbon ribs with high-strength aluminum wing skins still triggered a costly cracking crisis in 2012. Tiny assembly gaps stressed internal wing brackets until they split, forcing expensive fleetwide repairs. Airbus executive Richard Carcaillet explained to AIN Online: "The solution involves replacing the current wing rib feet—L-shaped brackets that attach the wing ribs to the skins made with the comparatively new, Alcan 7449 aluminum alloy—with rib feet made from slightly heavier, 7010 aluminum used in the A330.".

    Airbus absorbed over $330 million in wing-crack repairs across a $25 billion program that never broke even. Enders admitted to Bloomberg in July 2012: "Airbus thought it understood the properties of the A380 wing materials and the interface between carbon fiber and metal, but found out the wrong way we didn't know everything. It has cost the company a great deal of money and [harmed our] reputation." Yet Emirates turned that troubled airframe into an unmatched moneymaker.

    According to recent reports, twin decks give Emirates 5,920 square feet (550 square meters) of floor space, letting Dubai install onboard bars, showers, and upstairs premium economy cabins no twinjet could spare. Clark explained to the Points Guy in 2019: "Why was it that it was Emirates, who took it after Singapore Airlines, that it lit up the planet in terms of showers and bars and big TV screens? We did it for a very well-calculated reason... we had taken a huge risk and huge investment.".

    It has been revealed that cash-rich and parts-hungry, Emirates invested $5 billion in cabin refits, bought out 29 leased superjumbos, and agreed in November to acquire six more from Qatar's Lesha Bank. Teardown math drives that buying spree: used A380-800s trade cheaply, while one fresh landing gear set or four serviceable engines cost nearly as much as a complete plane. Dubai is cannibalizing its earliest retired frames for spares as Airbus factory support winds down.

    The concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

    While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a new restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

    Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.
